title: F5 · The factory
summary: The whole cell running a production shift: random arrivals, touching items, the vision-only cell and the learned carry, with an operator dashboard of live KPIs and a one-page operations report.

p: A shift: the line runs without stopping for ten minutes while items arrive at random, a quarter of them as two items touching (clutter, level L3 of the difficulty ladder in docs/sorting-cell-spec.md). Everything is on: the overhead camera is the only source of where things are (F4), the hybrid gripper uses its suction cup for flat boxes, the carry is the learned vision-only student, and the safety layer stops and recovers the robot when something goes wrong.

Every simulated second the cell writes its KPIs (key performance indicators), and the operator dashboard shows them live next to the camera stream: throughput, sort rate, where every item went, and OEE.

OEE (overall equipment effectiveness) is the number factories run on: availability (was the machine running?) x performance (did it keep up with the demand?) x quality (was the output good?). For a sorter: availability = share of time not stopped or recovering; performance = items the robot handled out of all that arrived; quality = of those, the share in the right chute.

blurb.h: Why does a robotics engineer care?
p: A demo is one pick; a factory is ten thousand. Over a shift the rare things happen: two items arrive together, a bottle tips, a burst of arrivals outruns the arm. The KPIs say which loss is the big one, and that decides what to engineer next.

Splitting touching items is a classic perception problem. Two items touching become one depth blob that looks like no single item. The fix here is classical: when a blob is unlike every item the identity model knows, cut it at its separate top surfaces (markers where the height is within 6 mm of its local maximum, then a watershed on the height map) and keep the cut only if every part now looks like an item.

Operations is a trade-off, not a maximum. A faster belt or more arrivals raise throughput until the arm saturates, then only add misses. Which point to run at depends on what a sorted item is worth and what a missed one costs: that is the operations report's job.
Touching pairs on a stopped belt: both items named in 59 of 60 pairs with the split, 41 of 60 without; 0 wrong names with the split, 1 without (factory/vision/results/f5-clutter-perception.json).
The shift and the operating envelope (belt 0.15, 0.3 and the fast 0.5 m/s, 8-16 arrivals per minute, with and without clutter): see the tables below and the operations report.
Start a short shift with the button below and watch the dashboard fill in. Push the arrival rate to 20 per minute and watch performance (not quality) collapse: the arm is the bottleneck.
Set clutter to 100%: every arrival is a touching pair. Then try the privileged perception to see how much of the loss is perception and how much is one arm facing two items.
Harder: a second arm downstream (F8 in docs/sorting-cell-spec.md) would take what the first one lets pass. Where would you put it, and how would the scheduler share the work?
